one_liner: Multi-threaded C key-value server speaking the Redis protocol (string commands only); out-scales single-threaded Redis on many-core Linux.
what_it_does: cachegrand is a standalone server, not a library: applications talk to it with ordinary Redis clients over RESP, with optional TLS/mTLS and a Prometheus metrics endpoint. It implements about 53 Redis string and keyspace commands (GET/SET/MGET/INCR/EXPIRE/SCAN/SELECT and similar), RDB snapshots via SAVE/BGSAVE, and LRU/LFU/random/TTL eviction. It has no lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, pub/sub, MULTI/EXEC, Lua, replication or cluster mode, and the Kafka, Memcache and WebAssembly features the README advertises are plans, not code.
how_it_is_fast: It runs one pinned worker thread per core; each worker multiplexes connections as user-space fibers (hand-written x86-64/aarch64 context switch) over io_uring, so there is no thread per connection and few syscalls. All workers share one multi-producer/multi-consumer open-addressing hashtable that packs 14 32-bit slot IDs (filled bit, probe distance, 16-bit hash fragment) into each 64-byte cache line, a layout borrowed from Folly's F14. It probes at most 32 neighbouring lines and compares a whole line with two AVX2 compares; AVX-512F, AVX, NEON and scalar variants are chosen at startup through GNU ifunc. Writes take a small spinlock per 14-slot chunk, so contention is spread across the table instead of behind one global lock, and memory comes from mimalloc with optional 2 MB hugepages.
when_to_use: String-only Redis workloads (GET/SET/MGET/INCR/EXPIRE on small values; the vendor test used 128 B) that need more throughput than one Redis process gives, where you would rather not shard across several Redis instances.

Many concurrent client connections hitting a many-core Linux x86-64 or aarch64 server (kernel 5.7+ for io_uring) on which you can dedicate cores, pin NIC queues and grant hugepages and unlimited memlock.
A cache with a known keyspace ceiling: the hashtable is sized up front from database.limits.hard.max_keys, which suits workloads whose maximum key count you can set in advance.
Studying or vendoring a BSD-3-Clause C implementation of a cache-line-packed SIMD concurrent hashtable, fibers and io_uring networking.
when_not_to_use: Anything beyond Redis strings and keys: other data types, pub/sub, MULTI/EXEC, Lua/functions, replication and cluster mode are missing, and the transactions and cluster-mode issues are still open.

Single-client or pipelined traffic. In the vendor data it is only about 1.1x Redis at one memtier thread without pipelining, and with pipeline=64 Redis 7.0.11 beat it on SET (386K vs 273K ops/s per load node).

Production systems that need an active upstream. There has been no release since v0.4.0 (May 2023), the last commit was 2025-01-02, and the expiry tests for SET/SETEX/PSETEX/GETEX were commented out as broken in December 2024.
Non-Linux hosts, older kernels, or sandboxes and containers that block io_uring or high memlock limits; io_uring is the only network backend.
A keyspace that can grow past a preset limit. There is no online resize (storage_db hard-codes can_auto_resize = false), and the memory limit does not count key bytes (open issue #439).

integration.form: standalone server binary (CMake build from source or the cachegrand/cachegrand-server Docker image); not a library
integration.dependencies: liburing, libnuma, libyaml/libcyaml, mbedTLS >= 2.28, libcurl, pcre2, json-c, liblzf, libatomic, mimalloc, t1ha/xxHash (several vendored under 3rdparty); hiredis only for tests; optional sentry
integration.min_toolchain: GCC (the build docs require gcc; the README's sample log shows gcc 11.3.0), CMake 3.16+, C11 (C++17 for tests and benches), Linux kernel 5.7+
integration.platforms: Linux only: x86-64 (runtime dispatch across AVX-512F/AVX2/AVX/scalar) and aarch64 (NEON)
integration.thread_safety: Server-level. All workers share one database. Hashtable writes take per-chunk (14-slot) spinlocks, and since PR #434 (Oct 2023) reads take per-chunk read locks inside a transaction.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — speaks RESP and implements about 53 string/keyspace commands plus RDB snapshots, so unmodified clients work for GET/SET-style caching; clients using other data types, pub/sub, transactions, scripting, replication or cluster will fail

gotchas: The hashtable size is fixed at start: the next power of two of database.limits.hard.max_keys (default 1,000,000). Probing stops after 32 cache lines (448 slots), so once a neighbourhood fills, inserts fail instead of the table resizing.

The skeleton config binds 0.0.0.0 and :: on 6379/6380 with require_authentication: false and max_clients: 100. If you turn on sentry, it uploads crash minidumps, which may contain stored data, to the author's sentry.io DSN by default.
The hashtable doc and the v0.2.1 benchmark describe lock-free, fence-based GETs. Since PR #434 (Oct 2023) GETs take per-chunk read spinlocks, and current main has not been re-benchmarked.

It needs high memlock and nofile ulimits (io_uring shares locked memory with the kernel) and preferably 2 MB hugepages. The performance docs also tell you to pin NIC IRQ/XPS queues per worker and disable irqbalance to approach the published numbers.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Dragonfly and KeyDB also serve the Redis protocol from many threads but cover far more of the command set and are maintained; Valkey is the maintained Redis fork. Pick cachegrand only for a GET/SET-only cache where its own data showing it ahead of Dragonfly v1.1.2 matters (about 1.4x GET and 1.25x SET at 64 memtier threads, about 3x GET with pipelining), or when you want a small BSD C hashtable and io_uring design to study or vendor.
verified_claims_summary: Vendor memtier_benchmark runs (128 B values, Gaussian keys over a 1M-key range, 25 connections per memtier thread, two load servers) on an AMD EPYC 7502P 32c/64t with bonded 2x25GbE and Ubuntu 22.04 measured cachegrand v0.2.1 at 935.6K GET ops/s per load node with 16 client threads against Redis 7.0.11's 71.1K with 1 client thread (about 13x). At equal single-thread load it was only 78.8K vs 71.1K (about 1.1x), and Redis was never run with more client threads or as multiple instances; both were built from source by the prep script (cachegrand as a CMake Release build, which is -O2, with t1ha2; Redis with a plain make), but the GCC version and the server configs are not published.
status_note: Stale since 2025-01-02, with no release after v0.4.0 (May 2023), about 1k stars and one main author; it is BSD-3-Clause and builds with CMake, but treat it as a research-grade server, not a production Redis replacement.
